text: Every automation script you've written so far has been the one reaching out, polling an API on a timer. A webhook flips that model: the security tool itself makes an outbound POST to a URL you control the instant something happens. That cuts the delay between a real event and your automation's reaction from minutes down to seconds, and it stops you from burning rate limit just to hear 'nothing changed.' But it also means your receiver is now a reachable endpoint, which changes what you have to defend.

The flow has three stages, in order. First, the tool fires an event and POSTs it to your receiver. Second, your receiver verifies that POST really came from that tool, by recomputing an HMAC signature over the raw request body and comparing it to a header the sender attached. Third, before any real processing runs, you check whether you've already handled this exact event ID — because webhook delivery is not guaranteed to be exactly-once.

A webhook receiver is just a small Flask app with one route. It pulls the JSON body, and critically, it responds fast — a 202 Accepted — rather than doing all the real work inline. Most senders use a short timeout, and a slow response gets marked failed and retried, which is exactly the kind of duplicate delivery your idempotency check exists to survive. The real work goes into its own function so it's testable without a running server.

Verification has to happen against the raw request bytes, not the parsed-and-reserialized JSON, because re-serializing can reorder keys and break the match even on a legitimate request. Use hmac.compare_digest for the comparison, never a plain equals sign — compare_digest runs in constant time, so response timing can't leak how many signature bytes matched. Only after that check passes do you look at the event ID against your set of already-processed events, and skip it if you've seen it before.

That's the full pattern: verify the signature against raw bytes, respond fast, then dedupe by event ID before any side effect runs. In production, that dedupe set becomes a database row or a Redis key with a TTL, so it survives restarts and works across multiple receiver instances. Next lesson, you'll put a verified webhook event to work — turning it into a real ticket in a case-management system, without creating a duplicate case on every retry.
